Photo sessions

How to shoot

Front photo every session. Add 45 and 90 degree views if the study needs them.

Same camera, same lens, same distance as the baseline. Neutral face. Hair back.

For wrinkles, add the frown, brow raise and squint photos, plus a close-up of each region you are scoring.

For a hollow, a tear trough or anything read off a shadow: front, both 45s, a close-up of each side straight on, and a close-up of each side at 45. Straight on, a hollow is almost all shadow and almost no shape. The 45 is where its depth shows.

Fix the light in one position, not just one brightness. Move a lamp and a hollow's shadow changes more than a filler will. The program measures exposure, left to right balance, hardness and white balance on every photo and tells you the per cent to change.

Scale

Which ruler is this using?

Face measurements come first. Measure one distance on the patient with calipers at the first visit. The program finds those two points by itself in every photo after that.

Ink dots are the alternative. A 1 cm pair is short. Being 1 or 2 pixels off at each end already puts you 3 to 4 percent out. Draw the pair 3 to 5 cm long instead and use the Custom pair chip.

Scale dots optional

Tracking dots same visit only

Ink dots inside the treatment area. They only work while the same physical dots are still on the skin.

Skin reference points

Moles, freckles and small scars. They move with the skin and they last for years. Mark the same ones every session.

Examiner grade 0 to 4

Settings

Both apply to every photo in the study. Set them at the first visit and do not change them again.
Blue is skin the lamp reflected off. It is left out of the reading because nothing can be read under a highlight.
Brow, lash and hairline inside the box are not skin. Dark hair against pale skin needs a lighter setting, since its shadow reaches further onto the forehead. Loose strands over skin are never found: mark the lines they cover with the pen, or erase them.
What the numbers mean

Area: how much of the region is covered by line.

Length: total line, end to end, and again per square centimeter of region.

N: how many separate lines were long enough to count.

Width: apparent width. Optical blur widens it, so read it as change and not as a true width.

Contrast: how much darker the lines are than the skin next to them.

Depth is not measured. A photo shows how dark a line is. Depth needs a replica or a 3D scan.
